en: Will the Chinese enjoy
Khan Kokotoy's abundant riches, uncle?
This poor soul has fallen into peril;
Will they bury us underfoot, uncle,
And thus mete out our punishment, uncle?
Should we present Maaniker, uncle,
And scatter all our wealth, uncle!
As dusk falls and the sun sets,
When the foremost of the people lie down to sleep,
Should we flee toward the Muslims, uncle?"
Then Koshoy said this:
"He who gives a feast bears blame, my son;
He who gathers the people bears guilt, my son!
On the downward slope the grass is thick, my son;
The infidels' people are many, my son.
On the upland the grass is sparse, my son;
The Muslim people are few, my son!
The Black Kalmyk and Manchu peoples,
As we have heard since ancient times,
Are enemies of the Muslims, my son!
There is much to say of it, my son;
When Manas migrated from Altai, my son,
There was a place where he slaughtered
The finest of the stone-bedecked Chinese, my son.
You did not stay quietly in Tashkent;
You drank your fill of liquor and ran wild, my son!
Saying, 'I will hold my father's memorial feast,'
You came merely to see the spectacle, my son;
Now you have seen calamity too, my son!
Submit to what he demands;
Give him Maaniker!
I long knew that the Kalmyks
I knew it long ago, my son!
Why did you provoke the obstinacy
Of leopard Manas the bloodletter, my son?
As for the humiliation wrought by the Chinese, my son,
If you heed me, then submit.
Take counsel with Manas;
If you give Maaniker, give him only then, my son!
Leopard Manas, bloodletter and lion,
Is the one whose fortunes are complete;
When you look within him,
He is broader than the face of the earth.
For the palmful of Muslims,
He is the hero who will protect them.
If that Manas does not come,
If he does not witness this oppression,
If he himself does not answer
The seething host of infidels,
The youngest of the six lions,
The servant beloved by God—
If lion Manas does not come,
The Chinese, numerous as cattle hairs,
Will trample us underfoot
And scatter all four kinds of livestock.
The countless Kalmyk people
Will bring about our end;
With accursed Joloy at their head,
They will slaughter every one
Of the Muslim sons.
You became rich and acted grandly;
Gathering all the people,
You brought humiliation on your own head, my son!
Send word to Talas;
Send it swiftly without delay
To the noble leopard Manas.
Tell Manas to come if he is a hero,
Tell him to unleash a great tumult,
And rescue the small band of Muslims
From the seething Chinese host.
Tell him to deliver them.
Say all the Black Kalmyks
Have reached us together at Tyup.
Say they raised their whole force
And utterly raided the Kyrgyz.
Say the Kalmyks bound
Your old hero Koshoy,
And utterly slaughtered
All the remaining giants!
Tell the valiant leopard Manas!
Wearing a blue lynx cap,
Wielding a mottled blue shield,
Khan Bakay, the rich man's son,
Who rests his head upon pure gold,
The resourceful sage—
Tell valiant old Bakay;
Tell all the valiant men!
Golden-crested, with a tasseled belt,
Only son of Khan Azezi in Beijing,
Who came and settled in Talas
And became Manas's companion—
Tell my leopard Almambet!
The peerless hero, born of Amyz,
Who rides a blue-gray horse,
Who wears a blue rapys coat—
Tell the gray-maned hero Chubak!
The finest of sixty,
The best of the forty companions,
Light on a horse and fit for a colt,
Sleepless and vigilant on the road,
The champion's support,
Khan Manas's hope—
Tell Syrgak, son of Ulak Khan!
Tell Shuutu with his tent-shaped kalpak;
Tell the old man like Kyrgylchal;
Tell all forty companions!
Say that it is Khan Kokotoy's memorial feast,
And that Kokotoy's Bokmurun
Has encamped at Karkyra.
Without sending word to you,
Say all the Muslims
Have put on black headdresses in mourning!
Say he must gird his waist firmly;
If bloodthirsty Manas the leopard
Is truly a valiant man,
Say he must pursue the seething Chinese
All the way to Beijing!
The measured time is six days;
Let him not delay beyond six days.
Go and say they have been left needing his aid.
Say the elders led by Koshoy
Have plundered
All the meat at the feast.
Say they have exerted their grieving strength;
The mighty Koshoy and Kongurbai,
From the hands of the Muslims,
Have seized every fine racehorse,
Leaving none at all.
Say they made the palace maidens who went strolling
Into captive women.
Say the servants who cooked the meat
Beat them with fire pokers,
And the witless Black Kalmyks
Slaughtered two thousand of them.
Say Kökötöy's son Bokmurun
Gathered the multitude
And held many festivities.
Without consulting Manas—
Say this was Bokmurun's appointed hour!
Without taking offense at that hour,
Say he must make the spectacle;
Dear brave Manas the leopard,
From the Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
The mere handful of Muslims—
Say he must rescue them.”
Brave Koshoy voiced his grief,
Giving six swift horses
And a palm-sized letter.
When the sun sank trembling,
When the Black Kalmyks and many Manchus
Lay gathered in a mass,
Thrown into confusion,
When they all dismounted together,
When all their chiefs
Lay there without making a sound,
Saying that no man would now travel,
The brazen Chinese
Fired their bellowing cannon.
Counting them less than his boot heel,
The Chinese lay there resounding.
Saying, “We have taken the Burut as plunder;
At the very feast we plundered the Burut
And have now put an end to them,”
They played their horns and trumpets.
With old Koshoy at their head,
I saw where they grieved;
I saw where the Black Kalmyks
And many Manchus rejoiced.
The mere handful of Muslims
Gathered together,
Saying the great Chinese would devour them on sight.
The Muslims stumbled about
And fled together,
Terrified and alarmed.
They saddled Maaniker
And put on the mail coat.
Without letting one person know,
Without making one person aware,
They mounted him on Maaniker.
Before the Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
I saw the great mass of Muslims
Cower in fear.
Sending him out like thieves,
To princely Manas the lion,
By night they sent Aydar—
I saw them send him.
With Khan Koshoy at their head,
With heroic Töshtük among them,
I saw where they panicked.
Infidels countless as hairs on a cow,
Swarming like ants—
I saw the ground they covered.
Their great city is called Beijing;
The Chinese are a people of forty khans.
At Kökötöy's memorial feast,
I cast my eye over the multitude
And took the measure of their numbers.
My side-locks were upon my head,
And I myself was six years old.
They mounted me on a dappled bay pacer,
Dressed me in a robe of silk,
And led little me pounding along
To the feast.
The people filled the land and seethed;
Infidels and Muslims
Crossed paths and swarmed
Along the banks of Karkyra,
At Khan Kökötöy's feast,
Below Aygyr-Zhal,
In the hollow of Ükürchü,
Along Üch-Kapkak,
Before the assembled people,
At Khan Kökötöy's memorial feast.
The people filled the land in crowds;
Dust flew into the sky.
When I looked over the people,
When I looked toward sunset,
The seething multitude
Was on the heights of Kyzyl-Kyya.
When I looked toward sunrise,
The seething multitude
Was along Chöl-Adyr.
In the hollows of Charyn and Ketmen,
Those of the army who could not fit
Were on the face of Chong-Kegen.
The great army on the rearward side
Was at the upper edge of Teek.
Those of the great army who could not fit
Were among Karkyra's pines,
Upon the pine-clad slopes.
The southern side of the gathering
Was along Aygay-Tash.
Then young Aydar with flowing forelocks,
Wearing a coat like mail,
Riding a horse like Maaniker,
Skimmed over the face of the earth.
Among every son of man who had heard,
He visited each without omission.
He traveled by day and night,
Went far without sparing his horse,
Never stopping overnight on the way,
Never resting or catching his breath.
He reached Talas
And now prepared to deliver the message
To princely Manas the leopard.
Young Aydar with flowing forelocks
Had circled and traveled
The four corners of the whole world;
He was the man who carried the news.
Khan Manas had been left without word;
The burden weighed upon his mortal soul,
And now the messenger arrived.
Manas had been left without news
Because, drunk on his countless livestock,
Ill-fated Bokmurun
Had sent him no message.
